explanations.explanation: Micah says it plainly: “At morning’s light they accomplish it because the power is in their hands.” No sleeping on it, no second thoughts. The plan that starts on the pillow is finished before the coffee gets cold. That's why Micah opens with a woe, friend.

I wish, friend! Most of my big late-night ideas, like baking ten dozen cookies before sunrise, are gone by breakfast. But Micah 2:1 says these people "accomplish it" when the morning light comes. The scheme doesn't fade, it gets done.

explanations.answer: They talk themselves out of it
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice twist, but the text doesn't give us any second thoughts. Micah says that at morning's light "they accomplish it." The power is in their hands, and the plan goes straight from bed to action.

Micah 2:2 says, "They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses." First they want it, then they grab it. Wanting something that's not yours is where the whole thing starts, friend. The power in their hands just finishes the job.
Planting would be honest work, and I'd happily help! But these folks aren't growing anything. Micah 2:2 says they "covet fields and seize them." They take fields that already belong to someone else.
Guarding a field is a fine job, friend. These people are doing the opposite. Micah 2:2 says they "covet fields and seize them," and they take away houses too. They aren't protecting anybody's land.

That's it. The LORD says, "I am planning against this nation a disaster from which you cannot free your necks." Picture a collar you can't wriggle out of, friend. These schemers spent the night planning, and now the LORD declares His own plan.

explanations.answer: A warning they are free to ignore
explanations.explanation: A warning you can ignore would be a gentle thing, but that's not what the LORD says. He calls it "a disaster from which you cannot free your necks." Ignoring it won't get them out. The text says they can't slip free.

explanations.answer: A short trial they can wait out
explanations.explanation: Waiting it out is what I did with a stuck drawer, friend. It doesn't work here. The LORD says it's "a disaster from which you cannot free your necks." Micah 2:3 gives no promise that it will be brief or easy to outlast.
Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity." The proud strut is gone when the calamity comes. Their power can't hold it back.
It's the other way around. In Micah 2:3 the LORD says, "Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity." So the proud walk stops. The calamity changes how they carry themselves.

That's what the lament says: "He has changed the portion of my people. How He has removed it from me!" A portion is the share of land that belonged to a family. Now the singers cry that it's taken away. Micah 2:4 says it, so we hear it as they do.
Thorns would be a sad end for a field, but Micah doesn't mention them here. The lament says, "How He has removed it from me!" The portion isn't overgrown. It's gone from them.
No water in this verse, friend. The lament says, "How He has removed it from me!" It goes on to say, "He has allotted our fields to traitors." So the portion has been taken away and given to others.

I can see why you'd think so, but Micah 2:5 says the opposite. It reads, "Therefore, you will have no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot." Nobody will be there to do it for them. The ones who seized other people's land lose their say.

Right. Micah 2:5 says, "Therefore, you will have no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot." Dividing land by lot is how shares were handed out. These people won't have anyone standing up there for them.

That's their confidence, friend. They say, "Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us." They're telling the preachers to stop because they're sure it can't touch them. Notice they never ask whether the message is true.

explanations.answer: The rains will come early this year
explanations.explanation: Rain would be great news for a field, but that's not what they say. The text gives their words: "Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us." What they're sure about is that disgrace won't reach them.

explanations.answer: The king will reward their plans
explanations.explanation: A king never comes up in these words. Micah 2:6 gives what they say: "Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us." Their confidence is about disgrace, not about any reward.

I get why the power talk might stick in your head after the last verses. But the LORD asks, "Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?" The good goes to the one who walks uprightly. The one with the most power doesn't get a bigger share.
Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?" Walking uprightly is what matters, and power doesn't. His words aren't something the strong can grab.

That's the word. The LORD says, "But of late My people have risen up like an enemy." These are His own people, and they're acting like an enemy toward each other. That's a hard thing to hear, so I'm glad you caught it.

A shepherd looks after people, and that's the opposite of what's described here. The LORD says, "But of late My people have risen up like an enemy." Sheep and a flock do show up later in the chapter, but not in this verse.
A widow isn't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "But of late My people have risen up like an enemy." They aren't the ones being hurt here. They're the ones doing the hurting.

That's right. The LORD says, "You strip off the splendid robe from unsuspecting passersby like men returning from battle." The passersby weren't expecting a thing. They're just walking along, and somebody takes their robe.
Sandals aren't in the verse, friend. The LORD says, "You strip off the splendid robe from unsuspecting passersby." What gets taken is the splendid robe, from people who weren't expecting it.

Swords are a fair guess because the verse mentions "men returning from battle." But that's the comparison for how they act. What they strip off the passersby is "the splendid robe," and these passersby are unsuspecting.

Yes. The LORD says, "You drive the women of My people from their pleasant homes." These are His people, and the homes are pleasant ones. I think this part is heavy, friend, so it's okay to just sit with it a second.
The verse says it directly. The LORD says, "You drive the women of My people from their pleasant homes." I think this one hurts to read. It's a heavy line, and it's in the text.

explanations.answer: This is not their place of rest
explanations.explanation: That's the reason given. The LORD says, "Arise and depart, for this is not your place of rest." The land they've been grabbing isn't a resting place for them. They won't settle in and relax there.

explanations.answer: A better land is waiting nearby
explanations.explanation: That would make for a nice moving day, friend. But Micah 2:10 doesn't mention a better land. It says, "Arise and depart, for this is not your place of rest." The reason is about the place they're in.
Enemies aren't mentioned in this verse. The reason given is, "for this is not your place of rest." The verse doesn't say when anything will happen, so I won't add a time.

explanations.answer: He'd be just the preacher for them
explanations.explanation: Micah says it with a bit of a sting: "he would be just the preacher for this people!" A man full of wind promising wine and strong drink is what they'd happily listen to. Meanwhile the real message gets told to stop. I think that's the sharpest line in the chapter, friend.

explanations.answer: They'd run him right out of town
explanations.explanation: They're the ones telling the real preachers to stop, so this doesn't fit. Micah says that a man of wind who falsely promises to preach about "wine and strong drink" "would be just the preacher for this people!" He'd be welcome, and nobody runs him off.

explanations.answer: They'd ask the prophets to test him
explanations.explanation: Testing him would be careful, but the text doesn't show that. It says he "would be just the preacher for this people!" They'd take a man of wind who preaches wine and strong drink and be glad to have him. No test is mentioned.

Yes, sheep. The LORD says, "I will bring them together like sheep in a pen, like a flock in the midst of its pasture." After all the hard words, this is a gathering. He says He will "surely gather" them and collect the remnant of Israel.
Horses are a fine animal, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "I will bring them together like sheep in a pen." A pen full of sheep is the picture of being gathered in.

I'd pay to see a camel in a pen, friend, but that's not the picture here. The LORD says, "I will bring them together like sheep in a pen, like a flock in the midst of its pasture." It's sheep, and the remnant is what He's gathering.
Not quite, friend. Micah 2:12 ends by calling the flock "a noisy throng." There's nothing quiet about a pen full of gathered sheep. The LORD says He'll bring them together, and they'll be loud.
Right. The verse ends with "a noisy throng." A whole flock packed in together is not a hushed room. The LORD gathers them anyway, noise and all.

That's the one. Micah 2:13 says, "One who breaks open the way will go up before them; they will break through the gate, and go out by it." Somebody goes ahead and opens the way, and they follow through. They don't have to push through alone.
Water isn't in this verse, friend. Micah 2:13 says, "they will break through the gate, and go out by it." The one who breaks open the way goes up before them, and then they go out by the gate.
No desert here. Micah 2:13 says, "they will break through the gate, and go out by it." That's where the way leads, with the one who breaks open the way going up in front.
Yes. Micah 2:13 says, "Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader." He goes first, and the flock follows. The remnant doesn't have to find the way out on its own.
Micah, the prophet who speaks these words, is the messenger here, not the leader. The verse says, "Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader." The LORD is the one in front.

Hezekiah was a king of Judah in Micah's days (Micah 1:1), but he isn't named in this verse. Micah 2:13 says, "Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader." The LORD Himself goes first.
